extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing research papers, expository articles, and textbooks (grad students, researchers, authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing mathematics and computer-science papers, expositions, and textbooks, covering exposition, presentation, examples, naming, and publication strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of formal and informal discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: An excellent exposition balances formal and informal discussion and uses well-chosen examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nilsson & Genesereth's chapter praised for its blend; useful when presenting a new area at graduate-student level. Use typography conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logic) to help clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motivating examples/puzzles to engage readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an example or puzzle that lets the reader see that the problem is non-trivial and that an algorithm might be possible; build the right mental structures before giving the algorithm or proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don used a puzzle to interest readers in a proof/algorithm. Be aware: illustrative algorithms may be inelegant but pedagogically useful. Avoid overwhelming the reader with too many cases; strive for unity where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful choice of terminology and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose names/terminology deliberately; names matter and can affect acceptance and later usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors sometimes regret names chosen (examples: LR(k) vs L(k), 'Daemon' vs 'Oracle'). Community feedback can prompt renaming (example of NP-complete replacing 'Polynomially-complete'). Consider consequences and be ready to change if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal selection criteria (research journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research journals publish results that are new, important, and significant contributions to the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those conditions are met, some leeway can be given in presentation quality; Journal of Algorithms is given as example. Align submission to journal's expectations (novelty, importance, significance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal selection criteria (expository journal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expository journals seek excellent mathematical exposition rather than primarily new results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Mathematical Monthly is cited as a home for excellent exposition; tailor submissions to exposition-focused venues if emphasis is clarity and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the reader's attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs to capture readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: attention-getting paper titles and opening paragraphs. Fame of author can help but do not rely on it alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell everything up front
rubrics_metrics.description: State in plain English what you are going to write about so readers can decide interest quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf: 'You can quintuple your readership if you will let them in on what it is that you are doing.' Be explicit about goals and results early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make papers scannable; highlight main results
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers scan for theorem statements and main results; make them easy to find and parse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize results using boldface (or other highlighting) so skimmers can latch on; avoid discursive-only pages. Drop notational abbreviations and convoluted references in theorem statements to aid skimming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation: use sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Some motivation is good, but readers dislike excessive motivation; too many failed-example motifs lose charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a small number of instructive motivating examples; don't overuse 'examples that do not yield desired results.' Avoid introducing mysteriously convenient starting points (e.g., 'Consider the following...') which often signal ad-hoc material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure proofs and exposition (chatty around lean proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be chatty and motivating before a proof, present the proof in lean and precise style, then be chatty again after the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf recommends conversational lead-in and follow-up with a rigorous, concise proof in the middle (Rudin-style proof). Use first-person where appropriate for exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust exposition length to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Different readers appreciate different levels of exposition density; condensed vs expanded treatments both have audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, dense expositions ('evidently') appeal to some; longer, more explanatory write-ups appeal to others. Decide which approach suits your target venue and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-authorship as quality filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use co-authors to filter idiosyncrasies and improve the book/paper's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff Ullman: co-authors won't save time but help curb eccentricities; filtering improves market competitiveness and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lots of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide many examples; even simple ones convey most of an idea, and later examples can refine details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff: 'Never saw a book with too many examples.' Finding good, focused examples is hard and time-consuming but high-value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put yourself in the reader's place
rubrics_metrics.description: Write from the reader's perspective: anticipate confusion and structure exposition accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try to remember what was hard to learn and address those points directly; this improves pedagogical order and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce exposition in the right order (read then write)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend time reading about a topic and then write it up later the same day to get the expository order right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff's tip: reading in the day and writing in the evening helps organize material in an order that matches a learner's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep definitions and uses close together; repeat if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defining things far away from their uses; repeat definitions when helpful for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff often sees definitions in Chapter 2 and use in Chapter 5—this mismatches readers' expectations. Repetition is acceptable to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target your exposition level; avoid opaque mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep exposition at a level readers can follow; when using powerful machinery, justify it and consider teaching needed background or deferring to references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoff example: spend many pages teaching asymptotic analysis vs. assume it and use references. Prefer to do basic calculations and avoid deep proofs if they would alienate intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: State variable types and avoid non-referential 'this'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the types of variables and avoid ambiguous referents like non-referential 'this'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactical remark: talk about 'the set S' not 'S'; Jeff's English professor forbade non-referential 'this'—it often bewilder readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition aims to educate, not to show off
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize teaching and clarity over showmanship or display of cleverness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quip: 'Those who can, do; those who can't, teach; those who can't teach, show off.' Keep focus on education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and imitation: be explicit and avoid verbatim copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation becomes culpable plagiarism when a reasonable person would believe you copied another's work; you cannot copyright ideas but can copy expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prentice-Hall guidance: if material appears too close to another work (identical italics, successive equations), it's suspect. In surveys, verbatim quotes are acceptable if clearly attributed; be explicit when quoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatics of book-writing (market and production)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider practical matters: sales targets, royalties, production costs, and editing time; pick a niche and aim for realistic market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff's back-of-envelope: ~1000 hours to write a book; typical CS book sales figures yield modest lifetime earnings; aim for 10,000 domestic sales by finding the right niche (be the hardest, easiest, or best book). Prepare camera-ready copy to lower publisher costs; second editions restart sales clocks but still require work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bad motives for writing papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write just to increase publication counts or to fit a particular conference; those motives can produce sloppy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie Lamport's warning: desire for long publication lists or to get into a specific proceedings are poor reasons and can lead to low-quality papers; write to disseminate accurate, worthwhile contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and metaphor judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy can aid exposition but should be used only when the reader will clearly get the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff encourages analogy where appropriate (physics texts do this often); ensure the analogy illuminates rather than confuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match style to venue and readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of editorial and community expectations about formality and style; some readers/editors object to informal styles creeping into formal venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf noted letters complaining about informal styles in journals. Choose level of formality to fit the journal (research vs expository) and audience expectations.
